# About this document {#sec-about .unnumbered}

A container image packs a program together with the operating system files,
libraries, and tools it runs on, so that it runs the same on a laptop, a
cluster, and in the cloud. For workflow code, an image is the usual way to pin
the environment of a step. This document says which tool to use where and
states the rules that hold for every image; the documents of the tools say
how. Its rules use the
[normative language](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-normative) of *Design
Principles*.

|  | [Apptainer](apptainer.qmd) | Docker |
|------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Runs as | The user, without root rights and without a daemon | A daemon with root rights |
| Where | HPC clusters and other shared Linux machines | Laptops, servers, continuous integration, the cloud |
| Image | One read-only SIF file | Layers in a local store or a registry |
| By default | Shares the home directory, the current directory, and the environment with the host | Isolated; shares only what is mounted |

Clusters allow Apptainer and rarely Docker, because the daemon of Docker gives
its users root rights on the machine. The two work together: Apptainer runs
images from Docker registries, so an image can be built with Docker, for
example in continuous integration, pushed to a registry, and run with
Apptainer on the cluster.

The principles already state the core of working with images: workflow code
runs every step in an image identified by its digest, together with the file
that builds it ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-pin)), and keeps that file,
and the image of a publication as well
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-recipe)). The rules below add what follows
from them for every image.


# At a glance {#sec-at-a-glance .unnumbered}

Every rule of this document in one line. The number and the title link to the
rule.

::: {.glance}
| No. | Rule | In one line |
|-----|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| [-@sec-pin] | [](#sec-pin) | Name the base image by its digest, and install packages with exact versions. |
| [-@sec-record] | [](#sec-record) | Record the digest or the checksum of the image with every result. |

# Rules {#sec-rules}


## Pin the base by digest, the packages by version {#sec-pin}

A recipe should name its base image by its digest, such as
`python:3.12-slim@sha256:…`, and install its packages with exact versions, for
example from a lock file. A tag such as `3.12-slim` or `latest` moves to a new
image with every update, and a package installed without a version is the
newest one: the same recipe then builds a different image next month, and
nothing shows it. With everything pinned, rebuilding gives the same software,
and an update is a change of the recipe that can be reviewed and tested.

Packages of the operating system, installed with `apt-get` or `dnf`, can often
not be pinned, because their archives keep only the newest versions. The image
itself is then the record of what was installed, which is one more reason to
keep the image that produced published results.


## Record the image with every result {#sec-record}

A result should record the image that produced it: the digest of a Docker
image, or the checksum of an Apptainer image file, such as the output of
`sha256sum analysis.sif`, next to the version of the code and the parameters
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)). A tag or a file name does
not identify an image, because both can point to another image tomorrow.
